<div class="box"><b>Case study:</b> Eeamtak et al., <i>Green Chemistry</i> (2026), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/d6gc03171d">10.1039/d6gc03171d</a><br><span class="small">A retrospective teaching reconstruction of a published review: how its review gap and novelty can be articulated. This is not a proposal to publish the same review again.</span></div>
<table><colgroup><col style="width:17%"><col style="width:15%"><col style="width:23%"><col style="width:23%"><col style="width:22%"></colgroup><thead><tr><th>Prior review</th><th>Window</th><th>Organising logic</th><th>What it does not do*</th><th>What we add</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><b>Harper et al.</b><br>2019, <i>Nature</i> [2]</td><td>Published 2019; search cutoff not stated in the material inspected.</td><td>EV lithium-ion battery reuse and recycling: assessment, disassembly, processing and design for recycling.</td><td>Does not organise the comparison using the combined reset-depth, repair-window and reversibility-ledger tools of this case study.</td><td>Link loss of structure at different scales to routes that preserve value for subsequent manufacturing.</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>Baum et al.</b><br>2022, <i>ACS Energy Lett.</i> [3]</td><td>Trend analysis: 2010-2021; not a cutoff for every claim.</td><td>Techniques, publication and patent trends, facilities, and economic and environmental issues.</td><td>A route overview does not itself supply a mechanistic rule matching differently degraded feedstocks to repair capability.</td><td>Explain why similar metal yields may leave different amounts of reusable structure and different rebuilding burdens.</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>Li et al.</b><br>2024, <i>Chem. Soc. Rev.</i> [4]</td><td>Published 2024; search window and cutoff not verified from the abstract.</td><td>Recycling fundamentals: classification, testing, pretreatment, electrolyte recovery and direct regeneration.</td><td>The inspected scope does not establish whether the same three-part decision tool is present. Audit the full text before claiming absence.</td><td>Connect knowledge across stages: feedstock state → reset depth → repairability → resource burden.</td></tr>
</tbody></table>
<div class="box tint"><h3>Example review-gap statement</h3><p>Relative to these selected reviews, there is room to synthesise <b>how the functional structure retained in a feedstock determines suitable recycling routes</b>, using descriptors that connect pack-level features to interphase chemistry and identify conditions under which direct regeneration remains selective.</p></div>
<p class="small">*The limitation column is a teaching interpretation of accessible material and the positioning in [1], not an exhaustive audit of all prior reviews. Earlier work already discusses material preservation and quality; do not claim that nobody previously considered structure.</p>
<p class="small"><b>Takeaway:</b> Publication year ≠ literature-search window. “What we add” should identify additional understanding or decision support, rather than simply more references.</p>

<section class="sheet" style="--accent:#12756e"><div class="eyebrow">MMS3 / Worked example / Worksheet B</div><h1 class="title">A completed one-page review proposal</h1><p class="subtitle">One-page proposal | Companion to Worksheet B, handout p. 9</p>
<div class="proposal">
<p class="small"><b>Status:</b> The title, concept and venue come from the published paper [1]. The year range, workflow, roles and schedule below are an <b>illustrative teaching plan</b>, not a record of the authors’ actual process.</p>
<div class="item"><h3>1. Working title</h3><p><b>Beyond metal recovery in lithium-ion battery recycling: order retention as a sustainability framework from pack disassembly to interphase chemistry</b></p></div>
<div class="item"><h3>2. Thesis - one sentence</h3><p>A suitable recycling route depends on matching <b>the order retained in the feedstock</b> to the process’s selective repair capability; metal recovery yield alone is therefore insufficient for route selection.</p></div>
<div class="item"><h3>3. Review type and target venue</h3><p><b>Critical review / conceptual synthesis; Green Chemistry.</b> The case study is already published as a Critical Review. For a new submission, check current journal requirements and overlap with existing reviews; do not invent unverified word or reference limits.</p></div>
<div class="item"><h3>4. Scope - Population, Concept, Context</h3><p><b>P:</b> Spent LIBs, focusing on LFP and layered-oxide cathodes; SIBs serve as a boundary comparison, without assuming identical behaviour. <b>C:</b> Order retention, reset depth and repairability. <b>C:</b> Recycling from pack disassembly to interphase chemistry. <b>Illustrative search years:</b> 2010-2026. Exclude lead-acid and primary batteries, and second-life operation unrelated to recycling-route selection. The actual paper does not report a systematic-review search window.</p></div>
<div class="item"><h3>5. Why now, and why us</h3><p><b>Why now:</b> Direct regeneration and varied feedstock states make it necessary to explain the value of retained structure and the burden of destroying and rebuilding it. <b>Why us:</b> The case-study team combines electrochemistry, materials and chemical engineering expertise, as described in [1]. Do not add unverified field-wide publication counts or a three-year publication record.</p></div>
<div class="item"><h3>6. Section outline - the organising framework</h3><p><b>Order-retention framework:</b> (1) Problem and prior-review gap → (2) Feedstock order descriptors → (3) Routes classified by reset depth → (4) Match disorder to repair windows through a reversibility ledger → (5) Reagent, energy, water and emissions implications → (6) Limitations and validation priorities.<br>Give each section a distinct role: material state / process / matching / impacts. Cross-reference evidence instead of retelling it.</p></div>
<div class="item"><h3>7. Deliverables and schedule - illustrative eight-week plan</h3><p><b>Targets:</b> About 80-100 references, four figures and three key tables: prior-review comparison / evidence matrix / descriptor-to-route map, with a search log and inclusion rules.<br><b>Roles:</b> Person 1 searches and extracts; person 2 checks numerical claims and primary sources; person 3 challenges mechanisms and conclusions. <b>Schedule:</b> W1-2 search/scope; W3-4 extract/appraise; W5-6 synthesise/draft; W7-8 verify/prepare submission. A 9 September 2026 start gives a target of 4 November 2026.</p></div>
</div>
<div class="box small"><b>PRISMA:</b> This critical-review example does not imply that the original paper used PRISMA. If a new project is designed as a scoping or systematic review, select the appropriate reporting guideline and record actual screening counts.</div>

<section class="sheet" style="--accent:#ab6d13"><div class="eyebrow">MMS3 / Worked example / Worksheet C / Evidence</div><h1 class="title">Read the evidence before writing the gap</h1><p class="subtitle">Worked evidence matrix | Five selected condition rows from Table 3 of [1]</p>
<div class="box small"><b>Evidence boundary:</b> These entries were extracted through Table 3 of [1], PDF p. 16, using its primary-reference numbers. This is a teaching extraction through a review. Check the primary papers and their test details before using the data in a research synthesis.</div>
<table><colgroup><col style="width:9%"><col style="width:23%"><col style="width:22%"><col style="width:28%"><col style="width:18%"></colgroup><thead><tr><th>ID</th><th>Feedstock / disorder</th><th>Route</th><th>Result reported in Table 3</th><th>Supported inference</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><b>E1</b><br>[5]<br>ref. 43</td><td>Degraded LFP: lithium loss, Fe(III)-rich surface and conductivity loss.</td><td>Direct regeneration with a multifunctional organic lithium salt.</td><td>Capacity increases from 102 to 157 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 C; 88% retention after 400 cycles.</td><td>Performance can recover without a complete structural reset in this case.</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>E2</b><br>[6]<br>ref. 57</td><td>Spent LFP slurry: lithium deficiency, with host framework retained.</td><td>Electrochemical relithiation; 25 °C, 2 h.</td><td>151.5 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 C; 96.6% retention after 400 cycles.</td><td>Some feedstock states permit restoration under mild conditions.</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>E3</b><br>[7]<br>ref. 59</td><td>LFP already dissolved into ionic species.</td><td>Acid leaching + hydrothermal synthesis.</td><td>136 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.1 C; 98.6% retention after 300 cycles at 1 C.</td><td>A functional product after deep reset does not imply preservation of the original structure.</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>E4</b><br>[8]<br>ref. 51</td><td>NMC622 with ionic Cu; best reported case at 0.34 at% Cu ion.</td><td>Reuse/regeneration of recovered cathode material.</td><td>Initial charge/discharge = 211.8/186.0 mAh g⁻¹ at 0.05 C.</td><td>Impurity chemistry matters; this value is not a universal Cu threshold.</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>E5</b><br>[8]<br>ref. 51</td><td>NMC622 with metallic Cu.</td><td>Reuse/regeneration tested in the same study as E4.</td><td>Table 3 reports that metallic Cu impurities can readily cause cell short circuits; this row gives no numerical threshold.</td><td>Total Cu alone cannot distinguish ionic from metallic impurity effects.</td></tr>
</tbody></table>
<div class="two"><div class="box"><h3>Evidence pattern</h3><p class="small">E1-E3: Post-recycling capacity alone does not reveal reset depth.<br>E4-E5: Impurity identity and chemical form affect reuse outcomes.</p></div><div class="box"><h3>How appraisal limits the claim</h3><p class="small">E4 and E5 come from one study, not two independent studies. Different C-rates, feedstocks and protocols prevent direct route ranking by capacity or retention.</p></div></div>
<p class="small"><b>Count correctly:</b> This excerpt has five condition rows from four primary studies. The full Table 3 has ten case/condition rows from eight references, not ten independent studies. Check replicates and controls in the originals; omission from this summary does not establish their absence.</p>

<section class="sheet" style="--accent:#ab6d13"><div class="eyebrow">MMS3 / Worked example / Worksheet C / Completed</div><h1 class="title">From evidence patterns to gaps and novelty</h1><p class="subtitle">Completed answers A-D | Companion to Worksheet C, handout p. 13</p>
<div class="box"><h3>A. Define the boundary</h3><p>Question: How do structural state and impurities in spent LFP/NMC cathodes help determine when direct repair is suitable and when a deeper reset is needed?</p><p class="small">Type: Critical synthesis in case study [1]. Evidence for this example: E1-E5, Fig. 4 and §4.5.6. Document inspection date: 9 September 2026. No new comprehensive database search was performed; this date is not a “last systematic search date”, and conclusions must remain within the selected evidence.</p></div>
<div class="box"><h3>B. Name the evidence pattern</h3><p>E1-E3 show that routes with different reset depths can each deliver usable performance under their own test conditions. E4-E5 show why Cu impurity forms must be distinguished. Section 4.5.6 describes numerical repair boundaries as working hypotheses drawn from heterogeneous sources and chemistries.</p><p class="small"><b>Still to check:</b> Comparisons using the same feedstock lot, pre-recycling disorder measurements, and comparable outcomes and controls. Reporting quality limits the strength of threshold claims.</p></div>
<div class="box tint"><h3>C. Research-gap statement - what the evidence cannot yet resolve</h3><p class="statement">Within the LFP/NMC evidence selected here, <b>transferable repair-window boundaries cannot yet be specified with confidence</b>. Starting material states, impurity forms and test protocols are not on a common basis, and the review’s numerical boundaries remain hypotheses requiring validation. This uncertainty affects the choice between direct regeneration and deeper-reset routes.</p><p><b>Research that would reduce the gap:</b> Split a single feedstock lot between direct regeneration and leaching/resynthesis; measure Cu speciation, structure and particle-size distribution before processing. Compare product purity, long-term cell performance, and energy/reagent burdens using the same functional unit and system boundary, with a justified number of replicates.</p></div>
<div class="box"><h3>D. Review-novelty statement - the understanding the review adds</h3><p class="statement">Relative to the selected reviews in Worksheet A, [1] adds <b>a mechanistic framework connecting order retention, reset depth, repair windows and a reversibility ledger</b>. Synthesising degradation states with recycling outcomes reframes route selection as matching feedstock condition to repair capability, making visible value that metal yield alone does not explain.</p><p class="small">This is the published review’s conceptual contribution. It does not establish that every threshold has been validated or that direct regeneration is superior under all conditions.</p></div>
<p class="small"><b>Reading Fig. 4:</b> The three blank cells in its 3 × 3 matrix indicate no worked feedstock examples in the map presented. They do not establish physical impossibility or prove that no relevant study exists anywhere in the literature.</p>

<section class="sheet" style="--accent:#12756e"><div class="eyebrow">MMS3 / Worked example / Teaching notes / Sources</div><h1 class="title">How to discuss the completed example</h1><p class="subtitle">Start with the purpose of the review, then identify the research still needed</p>
<div class="route"><span>A · What prior reviews leave unclear</span><span>→ B · What we will synthesise</span><span>→ C · What the evidence supports</span></div>
<div class="quote">“These two uses of ‘gap’ refer to different things. A review gap is something previous reviews have not adequately synthesised. A research gap is a question the research evidence cannot yet answer adequately. This paper adds an order-retention framework for thinking about recycling-route selection, but it does not turn every proposed threshold into a validated fact. That distinction explains both the review’s novelty and the starting point for further research.”</div>
<div class="three" style="margin-top:14px"><div class="box"><h3>Ask participants</h3><p class="small">If a recycled cathode achieves high capacity, can we conclude that its recycling route is the most sustainable?</p></div><div class="box"><h3>Expected response</h3><p class="small">Not yet. Compare feedstock, durability and resource burdens on a common basis.</p></div><div class="box"><h3>Writing prompt</h3><p class="small">Choose one E1-E5 pattern. Write a one-sentence gap and specify a comparator and outcome that would reduce the uncertainty.</p></div></div>
